# AI Agent Guidelines for "The Pair"

This file contains instructions and context for any AI agents (like yourself) working on the `the-pair` repository.

## Project Identity

"The Pair" is a Desktop application built with Tauri 2.x, React 19, and TypeScript. It orchestrates two AI agents — a **Mentor** (planner/reviewer, read-only) and an **Executor** (code writer/command runner) — that cross-check each other's work. Each agent talks straight to a model endpoint over HTTP; the app manages their lifecycle, tracks token usage and cost, tracks git changes, and provides a polished UI for humans to observe and intervene.

## Tech Stack

- **Framework:** Tauri 2.0
- **Backend:** Rust
- **Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript
- **Styling:** Tailwind CSS v4, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge`
- **Icons:** `lucide-react`
- **State Management:** `zustand` (`usePairStore`, `useModelStore`, `useUpdateStore`, `useThemeStore`, `useLocaleStore`)
- **Animations:** Framer Motion

## Architecture Rules

1. **Rust Backend vs. React Frontend:**
   - Never import Node.js built-ins directly into the Renderer (`src/renderer/src/`).
   - Use Tauri commands in `src-tauri/src/` to expose strict APIs to the frontend.
   - Frontend calls backend via `invoke()` from `@tauri-apps/api/core`.
2. **Styling:**
   - Always use Tailwind CSS classes. Custom dark/light mode palette is defined in `src/renderer/src/assets/main.css`.
   - Shell chrome (sidebar, hub, inspector, modals, palette) uses sans (`font-sans`, Geist Sans/SF); the conversation core (pair stream, diffs, code) uses mono (`font-mono`, Geist Mono). Never re-mono shell labels or re-sans the stream — `tests/shellTypography.test.ts` pins the split.
   - Shell surfaces use `.shell-card` (+ `.shell-card-hover`); the sidebar rail uses `.app-source-list`. The stream stays flat with hairline borders.
   - Use the `cn()` utility from `src/renderer/src/lib/utils.ts` for conditional class merging.
3. **Agent Interactions:**
   - Every turn runs inside the app: `harness` drives the model over HTTP and runs the tools itself, so no agent CLI is ever spawned. Runs are unbounded by default (`maxIterations = 0`); an optional per-pair iteration cap pauses the pair into human review when reached — keep that cap semantics intact when touching turn logic.
   - Use the handoff guard (`src/renderer/src/lib/handoffGuard.ts`) to prevent race conditions when pairs finish.
4. **Error Handling:**
   - Handle permissions and locked files defensively in the Rust backend.
   - Propagate errors cleanly to the frontend via Tauri commands to display in the `ErrorDetailPanel`.

## Rust Backend Modules (`src-tauri/src/`)

| Module               | Responsibility                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pair_manager`       | Pair lifecycle: create, list, delete, pause, resume, assign task, update models; resolves each pair's workspace (in-place, or a fresh worktree on an auto-named `the-pair/…` branch — per task when requested)                                                                                                              |
| `message_broker`     | State machine for agent turn coordination and event routing; also flags stalled turns (warning at 120s without output, stalled at 600s)                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `context_bridge`     | Parses the mentor's plan checklist and bridges handoff context between mentor/executor turns                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `harness`            | One turn end to end on the direct connection: `driver.rs` (`TurnDriver`) owns turn orchestration and cancellation, `turn.rs` runs the request and falls back to the backup model, `resolve.rs` maps a pair's stored model string onto a registry selection, `history.rs` holds each (pair, role) conversation and bounds it |
| `accounts`           | Direct-connection model registry: providers `(protocol, base_url)`, accounts (API key / OAuth / env), model routes; persists `credentials.json` (0600) in the app data dir and serves the `accounts_*` commands                                                                                                             |
| `sources`            | Read-only importers that discover model configuration inside other agents' installs (kimi, pi, omp, opencode, codex, claude, gemini, killi, env); returns drafts, never writes                                                                                                                                              |
| `login`              | Subscription sign-in flows: ChatGPT (PKCE + loopback callback), Command Code (studio hand-off), opencode-go and Muse Code (pasted key); tokens cached per service under `app_data_dir/oauth/`                                                                                                                               |
| `llm`                | Direct HTTP transport: `Client::complete()` over 4 protocols (OpenAI Chat, Anthropic Messages, Responses, Command Code NDJSON) with retry/backoff, a shared 429 cooldown, and a cancellable delta stream                                                                                                                    |
| `tools`              | The executor's own tool loop: read / write / edit / bash / grep / glob + todo_write, gated per role by `ToolPolicy` (mentor read-only), with hard workspace path containment and no `regex`/`globset` dependency                                                                                                            |

| `smart_pause`        | Pause reasons (iteration budget exhausted) and the plan-approval gate decision; human-readable pause messages                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

| `report_generator`   | Session run reports (markdown + file export), written to the app data dir — never into the user's repository                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

| `path_env`           | Refreshes `$PATH` — and, with `sources/env.rs`, the rest of the login shell's environment — at startup: the executor's `bash` tool needs it to find `npm`/`cargo`, and env-backed accounts resolve their key from it at turn time                                                                                           |

## Pair Status State Machine

```
Idle → Mentoring → Executing → Reviewing → (loop or Finished)
                                         → Paused → (resume → Mentoring or Reviewing)
                                         → Awaiting Human Review
                                         → Error
```

## Session Snapshot & Recovery

Snapshots are persisted to Tauri's app data directory. Each snapshot includes full conversation history, agent activity, git tracking state, and provider session IDs. On restore, the appropriate resume prompt is injected so agents can continue from where they left off.

A pair on the direct connection also stores each agent's harness conversation (the OpenAI-shaped messages, including its tool calls) and the model selection it was talking to, both under `providerSessions`. Without them a restart would lose the endpoint the pair was talking to and never replay what it had already said. Snapshots written by older builds — including ones that still carry `mentorProvider`/`executorProvider` and per-agent CPU/memory samples — load as they are: serde ignores fields the current structs no longer have, and a pair whose stored model id resolves onto no endpoint fails its turn with a "pick one in the pair's settings" error instead of silently falling back.

## Adding Features

- **UI Components:** Keep components modular in `src/renderer/src/components/`. Reusable primitives go in `components/ui/`.
- **State:** Use `usePairStore` for pair-related global state. Add new stores in `src/renderer/src/store/` only if the concern is orthogonal.
- **Tauri Commands:** Add new commands to the appropriate Rust module and register them in `lib.rs`'s `invoke_handler`.
- **Models:** Update `accounts/presets.rs` when adding new model entries (display name, context/output limits, reasoning efforts, price); the registry merges imported and manual endpoints on top of them.

## Testing & Coverage

**Policy: new or changed code must have 95%+ line coverage from unit tests.** Measured as _changed lines_ (`git diff`) against the coverage report, not whole-repo averages.

Three layers, all headless except the optional desktop smoke:

| Layer               | Command                                                                                                                   | Covers                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rust unit tests     | `npm run test:rust` (in `cargo test`)                                                                                     | `PairManager`/broker/driver logic, git worktree operations against real temp git repos |
| Renderer unit tests | `npm run test:js` (store/logic, `tests/*.test.ts`) + `npm run test:ui` (jsdom component tests, `tests/render/*.test.tsx`) | Store contracts, modal/branch-chip UI                                                  |
| Headless e2e        | `npm run e2e:web` (Playwright + a scripted Tauri IPC mock, `e2e-web/`)                                                    | Real app UI against a mocked backend                                                   |
| Desktop e2e         | `npm run e2e` (Appium mac2, needs a GUI machine)                                                                          | Real packaged app, on-demand only                                                      |

Coverage commands:

- `npm run coverage:ts` — c8 report for the renderer (runs both unit suites).
- `npm run coverage:rust` — `cargo llvm-cov` for the Rust lib.

Harness notes:

- **Renderer component tests** (`tests/render/`) run React under jsdom via `node:test` + `@testing-library/react`. They use `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=tsconfig.web.json` (through `scripts/with-env.mjs`) so tsx applies the automatic JSX transform — component modules rely on it. `tests/render/setup-dom.ts` installs the jsdom globals and the `__APP_VERSION__` vite define; `tests/render/mock-ipc.ts` installs the real `tauri-shim` plus a scripted `mockIPC` handler covering `repo_check_state` and friends.
- **Headless e2e** (`e2e-web/`) starts the vite dev server (`npm run dev:renderer -- --port 5199 --host 127.0.0.1`) and injects `e2e-web/mock-init.js` before app code, defining `window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__`/`__TAURI_EVENT_PLUGIN_INTERNALS__`. Every IPC call lands on `window.__MOCK_CALLS__` so specs assert exact payloads. Test state is seeded through `openApp(page, state)` in `e2e-web/fixtures/app.ts`.
- **Local UI inspection:** When eyeballing the running dev server, try **moli first**, Chrome/Chromium only as a fallback. Read the page with `moli fetch --dump markdown http://127.0.0.1:5199`; add `--layout` for a rendered screenshot. Fall back to a Chrome/Chromium browser only when moli cannot cover the check.
- Keep tauri command bodies thin: extract the testable logic into plain functions (see `prepare_new_run_workspace`, `prepare_run_context`, `validate_assign_task` in `pair_manager.rs`) — command shells cannot be unit-covered without an app runtime.

## Release Process (Automated)

**⚠️ CRITICAL: Never manually create or push git tags!**

The release workflow (`build-signed-mac.yml`) is fully automated:

1. **Prepare release:**
   - Bump the version with `npm run bump <version>` — it updates `package.json`, the root entries of `package-lock.json`, the `[package]` version in `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and the app entry in `src-tauri/Cargo.lock` (`tauri.conf.json` reads its version from `package.json`)
   - Update `CHANGELOG.md` with release notes under a `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` heading at the start of a line (`npm run validate:changelog` checks it; the release workflow uses the same matcher, `scripts/changelog.mjs`, for its gate and for the release notes)
   - Run quality gates locally: `npm test && npm run typecheck && npm run lint`

2. **Publish:**
   - Commit changes: `git commit -m "chore: bump version to X.Y.Z"`
   - Push to main: `git push`
   - **Do NOT run `git tag` or `git push --tags`**

3. **Workflow automation:**
   - GitHub Actions inspects the version's tag and release; only a complete public release is skipped, while incomplete states fail for manual inspection
   - Release runs are serialized and never cancelled mid-run, but GitHub may replace a pending run with a newer one
   - Builds macOS, Windows, Linux binaries after parallel frontend and Rust checks
   - Creates tag `vX.Y.Z` on the pushed commit and a draft release with the changelog section as notes
   - Verifies updater signatures against the configured public key, then compares uploaded asset SHA-256 digests before publishing; never overwrites existing releases or assets

4. **Verify:**
   - Monitor at: https://github.com/timwuhaotian/the-pair/actions
   - Check release page for correct artifacts and notes

### Version Bump Guidance

Follow Semantic Versioning (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`):

| Keyword           | Bump   | When to use                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **patch release** | `Z` +1 | Bug fixes, docs updates, typo corrections, internal refactors (no API change) |
| **minor release** | `Y` +1 | New features, new components, new Tauri commands (backward-compatible)        |
| **major release** | `X` +1 | Breaking changes, UI redesigns, removed APIs, state machine changes           |

**Quick decision tree:**

- `fix:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `style:` → **patch** (e.g. 2.0.0 → 2.0.1)
- `feat:` without breaking changes → **minor** (e.g. 2.0.0 → 2.1.0)
- `feat:` with breaking changes, or removing public APIs → **major** (e.g. 2.0.0 → 3.0.0)

**Fallback:** If workflow fails to trigger, run:

```bash
gh workflow run build-signed-mac.yml
```

See `docs/RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` for detailed checklist.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

`AGENTS.md` contains the longer architectural reference (module table, component table, state machine, release process). Read it when you need that depth; this file covers the essentials for getting productive fast.

## What this app is

The Pair is a Tauri 2 desktop app (Rust backend, React 19 + TypeScript frontend) that orchestrates two AI agents working together on a coding task:

- **Mentor** — read-only planner/reviewer
- **Executor** — code writer / command runner

The Rust backend talks to model endpoints directly over HTTP — no agent CLI is spawned. It streams each reply, runs the tools the model asks for (`read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`, `grep`, `glob`, `todo_write`) inside the pair's workspace, runs a turn-based state machine, and tracks git changes. The React frontend renders the conversation, status, and controls.

### How frontend talks to backend

Always go through `src/renderer/src/lib/tauri-api.ts`, which wraps `invoke()` from `@tauri-apps/api/core` with typed helpers. The renderer never imports Node built-ins; the only escape hatch is `tauri-shim.ts`, which provides safe fallbacks when running under `npm run dev:renderer` (no Tauri host).

### Adding a Tauri command

1. Implement `#[tauri::command]` in the appropriate `src-tauri/src/<module>.rs`.
2. Add the function to the `tauri::generate_handler![]` list in `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`.
3. Add a typed wrapper in `src/renderer/src/lib/tauri-api.ts`.
4. Cover with a unit test in `tests/` (pure logic) and/or a Rust test in the module file.

### State machine

`Idle → Mentoring → Executing → Reviewing → (loop | Finished | Paused | Awaiting Human Review | Error)`

Pairs hit an `iteration_limit` and pause for human review rather than running unbounded. `src/renderer/src/lib/handoffGuard.ts` prevents duplicate handoff events firing after a pair finishes — keep using it when adding new transition logic.

### Model endpoints

A pair's mentor and executor each store a model id. `harness/resolve.rs` maps it onto a registry selection — an endpoint, an account and the endpoint's own spelling of the id — preferring the endpoint the model was picked under, and a role keeps its endpoint across handoffs while that endpoint can still run the model. Endpoints and credentials live in the registry (`accounts/`), filled by the importers in `sources/`, the sign-in flows in `login/`, or by hand in the Models section. Each endpoint speaks one of four wire protocols, implemented under `llm/`. When adding a model, update `accounts/presets.rs`; when adding a protocol, add a module under `llm/` and a `Protocol` variant in `accounts/types.rs`.

## Conventions

- **TypeScript only** in the renderer — no `.js` files, no `any`. Use `interface` for object shapes, export shared types from a local `types.ts`.
- **Tailwind v4 only** for styling — no inline styles, no CSS modules. Use `cn()` from `src/renderer/src/lib/utils.ts` to merge classes. Theme tokens are defined in `src/renderer/src/assets/main.css`.
- **Zustand** for global state; component-level state via hooks. Keep stores minimal — derive computed values rather than caching them.
- **Path aliases**: `@renderer/*` and `@/*` both map to `src/renderer/src/*` (see `vite.config.ts`).
- **Conventional Commits** for messages (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `style`). PRs are squash-merged.
- **Husky + lint-staged** run `eslint --fix` and `prettier --write` on staged files on commit. Do not use `--no-verify` unless explicitly asked.

## Mock mode

Set `THE_PAIR_E2E_MOCK=true` (e.g. via `npm run dev:mock`) to replay canned turns instead of calling a model; the registry also gains two mock endpoints, so a pair can be created with no credential on the machine. `THE_PAIR_E2E_MOCK_SCENARIO=dev-smoke` seeds a richer mock dataset. This is the path used by e2e specs and is useful when iterating on UI without an API key.

## Releases — DO NOT push tags manually

GitHub Actions (`build-signed-mac.yml`) auto-tags and publishes when a version bump lands on `main`. The full flow:

1. `npm run bump <version>` (updates `package.json`, the root entries of `package-lock.json`, the `[package]` version in `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and the app entry in `src-tauri/Cargo.lock` in lock-step; `tauri.conf.json` reads its version from `package.json`)
2. Update `CHANGELOG.md` — the heading must start its line as `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` and the section must not be empty (the release gate and the release-notes extraction share `scripts/changelog.mjs`)
3. Run `npm test && npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm run build`
4. `git commit -m "chore: bump version to X.Y.Z"` and `git push` — that's it

Never run `git tag` or `git push --tags`. The workflow tags the pushed commit (`--target $GITHUB_SHA`), runs one release at a time (a run queued behind a release skips once the tag exists), and fails rather than overwrite an existing release. Fallback if the workflow misses the bump: `gh workflow run build-signed-mac.yml`. See `docs/RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md`.

### Version bump keywords (semantic versioning)

When deciding which version part to bump:

| Conventional commit type                                           | Release type      | Version bump           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| `fix:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `style:`                                | **patch release** | `Z` +1 (2.0.0 → 2.0.1) |
| `feat:` (backward-compatible)                                      | **minor release** | `Y` +1 (2.0.0 → 2.1.0) |
| `feat:` with breaking changes, API removals, state machine changes | **major release** | `X` +1 (2.0.0 → 3.0.0) |

**Rule of thumb:** If you're only fixing bugs, updating docs, or doing internal refactors → patch. If you're adding new features/components/commands without breaking existing behavior → minor. If you're removing public APIs, redesigning the UI, or changing the state machine → major.

The Pair は無料でオープンソースですか？ はい。The Pair は Apache 2.0 ライセンスのオープンソースで、macOS・Windows・Linux 向けに無料でダウンロードできます。支払うのは自分のモデル利用料だけ — [Ollama](https://ollama.com) でローカルモデルを動かせば API コストはゼロです。
Cursor、GitHub Copilot、Aider の代わりになりますか？ はい。ただしアプローチが違います。それらのツールは単一のエージェントを動かします。The Pair は独立した 2 つのエージェント — 読み取り専用の Mentor と Executor — が相互に検証するので、ミスは出荷される前に 2 つ目のモデルが捕まえます。ローカルファーストで、オープンソースで、モデル非依存です。
どのモデルが使えますか？ 接続したエンドポイントから到達できるモデルなら何でも — 他のエージェントの設定からインポートしたもの、手動で追加したもの、サブスクリプションでサインインしたもの — GPT、Claude、Gemini、Grok、GLM、Qwen、Kimi、MiniMax、DeepSeek、そして Ollama 経由のローカルモデルを含みます。Claude を Mentor に、GPT を Executor に、といった組み合わせも自由です。
インターネット接続は必要ですか？ アプリはローカルで動きます。接続が必要なのはモデル呼び出しだけで、Ollama ならそれすら不要です。
エージェントの「思考量」は調整できますか？ はい。対応しているモデルでは、Pair の作成時にも、あとから設定でも、Mentor と Executor の推論の強さを個別に設定できます。
エージェントが実際に何をしているか見えますか？ はい。各ターンには認知イベントのストリーム — インテントチップ、推論ステップ、各ツール呼び出しとその状態 — が表示されるので、生の出力を読まなくてもエージェントの考えを追えます。
トークンとコストはどう追跡しますか？ 使用量はターンごとに、入力と出力を分けて記録されます。ライブの数値はコンソール、インスペクター、エクスポートした実行レポートに表示されます。
エージェントがループにはまったら？ 実行は既定では無制限です。反復上限を設定しておくと、上限に達した時点で **人手レビュー待ち** に入り、続行・モデルの変更・終了を選べます。また、ターン内のステップサイクルガードが暴走したツールループを止めます。
アプリがクラッシュしたり、途中で閉じてしまったら？ セッションのスナップショットは自動的に保存されます。次回の起動時に The Pair が中断されたセッションを見つけ、履歴ごと復元するかを尋ねます。
自動でアップデートされますか？ はい。The Pair は起動時に新しいバージョンを確認し、ワンクリックでインストールします。

## 왜 에이전트가 둘인가 코드를 작성한 모델에게 자기 코드를 검토하게 하면 대개 스스로에게 동의합니다. The Pair는 이 일을 둘로 나누어 서로 다른 에이전트에게 — 원한다면 서로 다른 모델에게 — 맡깁니다. | 역할 | 하는 일 | 손댈 수 있는 범위 | | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | | **Mentor** | 코드를 읽고, 계획을 쓰고, 모든 결과를 검토합니다 | 읽기 전용 | | **Executor** | 코드를 쓰고, 명령을 실행하고, 검증한 뒤 결과를 넘깁니다 | 해당 Pair의 작업 공간뿐 | ```mermaid flowchart LR T([당신의 작업]) --> M[Mentor가 계획] M --> E[Executor가 작성·실행] E --> R[Mentor가 검토] R -- 보완 필요 --> M R -- 완료 --> F([완료]) R -. 반복 한도 .-> H([사람 검토 대기 중]) ``` 실행은 Mentor가 완료를 알리거나 당신이 멈출 때까지 계속됩니다. ## 기능 **루프** - **듀얼 에이전트 아키텍처** — 계획과 검토(Mentor)를 실행(Executor)과 분리 - **스마트 조율** — 구조화된 핸드오프 프롬프트, 품질 게이트, 스마트 일시 중지로 반복이 흐트러지지 않게 - **수락 검사** — Mentor가 테스트와 lint를 실행한 뒤 위험도, 근거, 다음 단계를 담은 판정을 반환 - **계획 게이트와 반복 한도** — 첫 계획을 직접 승인하도록 할 수 있고, Pair별 반복 한도도 설정 가능(기본은 무제한) - **정체 감지** — 출력이 120초 없으면 경고, 600초면 정체로 표시 **콘솔** - **하나의 세션 콘솔** — 작업, 계획, 결과, 검토, 실시간 턴을 하나의 스크롤 피드에. 검색과 역할 필터 포함 - **인지 이벤트 스트림** — 턴마다 인텐트 칩, 추론 단계, 도구 호출 상태 - **사용량 추적** — 턴별·실행별 토큰, 예상 비용, 요청 수, 마지막 출력 - **인스펙터** — 모델, 실행 상태, 사용량, 파일, 기록, 타임라인을 접을 수 있는 섹션으로 - **활동과 인사이트** — 모든 Pair 중 주의가 필요한 것, 그리고 잘 통했던 모델 조합 **당신의 저장소** - **Git 변경 추적** — 기준 커밋 대비 추가·수정·삭제된 파일을 파일별 인라인 diff와 함께 - **워크트리** — 작업마다 전용 git worktree와 `the-pair/…` 브랜치에서 실행하고, 인스펙터에서 바로 커밋과 푸시 - **스킬과 멘션** — `/skill`로 프로젝트 스킬 파일을, `@path`로 파일을 첨부 - **세션 복구** — 진행하면서 스냅샷을 저장하고, 중단된 세션은 기록과 턴 상태까지 되돌립니다 **모델** - **엔드포인트는 직접 가져오기** — 다른 에이전트의 설정(opencode, codex, claude, kimi, pi, omp, gemini, killi)을 가져오거나, 키를 직접 추가하거나, ChatGPT·Command Code·OpenCode Go·Muse Code 구독으로 로그인 - **어떤 모델이든 어느 역할에나** — Mentor와 Executor 각각의 엔드포인트, 모델, 추론 강도를 따로 선택 - **로컬 오케스트레이션** — 앱과 조율 로직은 내 컴퓨터에서 실행되고, 모델 호출은 선택한 엔드포인트나 로컬 모델로 직접 전송 **앱** - **명령 팔레트와 단축키** — 모든 동작에 닿는 ⌘K, 전역 단축키, 네이티브 메뉴 바 - **네 가지 언어** — English, 简体中文, 日本語, 한국어 - **라이트/다크 테마**, 한 번에 음소거할 수 있는 사운드 알림, 앱 내 업데이트 ## 설치 [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/timwuhaotian/the-pair/releases)에서 최신 버전을 다운로드하세요: | 플랫폼 | 파일 | | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | **macOS** | `the-pair-{version}.zip` | | **Windows** | `the-pair-{version}-setup.exe` | | **Linux** | `the-pair-{version}.AppImage.tar.gz` (압축을 풀고 AppImage 실행) | 터미널이 더 편하신가요? 인터넷 연결이 필요한가요? 앱은 로컬에서 실행됩니다. 연결이 필요한 것은 모델 호출뿐이고, Ollama를 쓰면 그것마저 필요 없습니다.
에이전트가 얼마나 "생각"할지 조절할 수 있나요? 네. 지원하는 모델이라면 Pair를 만들 때나 나중에 설정에서 Mentor와 Executor의 추론 강도를 따로 정할 수 있습니다.
에이전트가 실제로 무엇을 하는지 볼 수 있나요? 네. 각 턴에는 인지 이벤트 스트림 — 인텐트 칩, 추론 단계, 각 도구 호출과 그 상태 — 이 표시되므로, 원시 출력을 읽지 않고도 에이전트의 논리를 따라갈 수 있습니다.
토큰과 비용은 어떻게 추적하나요? 사용량은 턴 단위로, 입력과 출력을 나누어 기록됩니다. 실시간 수치는 콘솔, 인스펙터, 내보낸 실행 보고서에 나타납니다.

앱이 죽거나 세션 중에 닫아 버리면요? 세션 스냅샷은 자동으로 저장됩니다. 다음 실행 때 The Pair가 중단된 세션을 찾아 전체 기록과 함께 복원할지 묻습니다.
자동으로 업데이트되나요? 네. The Pair는 실행할 때 새 버전을 확인하고, 클릭 한 번으로 설치합니다.

## Why two agents A model that writes code and then reviews its own code tends to agree with itself. The Pair splits the job in two and gives each half to a different agent — and, if you like, a different model. | Role | What it does | What it can touch | | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | **Mentor** | Reads the code, writes the plan, reviews every result | Read-only | | **Executor** | Writes code, runs commands, verifies, hands the result back | The pair's workspace, nothing else | ```mermaid flowchart LR T([Your task]) --> M[Mentor plans] M --> E[Executor writes and runs] E --> R[Mentor reviews] R -- needs work --> M R -- done --> F([Finished]) R -. iteration cap .-> H([Awaiting human review]) ``` Runs continue until the Mentor signals completion or you stop them. Set an iteration cap on a pair and reaching it pauses the run for your review, so you can continue, reassign models, or finish. While they work, go grab a coffee — or stay and steer: you can stop a turn, send feedback, or approve the plan before a line is written. ### How it compares | Capability | The Pair | Cursor / Copilot | Claude Code (solo) | | ------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- | | Cross-validation between agents | ✅ Two independent agents | ❌ Single agent | ❌ Single agent | | Dedicated review role | ✅ Mentor (read-only) | ❌ Self-review only | ❌ Self-review only | | Multi-provider support | ✅ Any model endpoint | ❌ Locked to one | ❌ Claude only | | Local orchestration | ✅ Fully local | ❌ Cloud-dependent | ❌ Cloud-dependent | | Session recovery | ✅ Full snapshot restore | ❌ | ❌ | | Open source | ✅ Apache 2.0 | ❌ Proprietary | ❌ Proprietary | ## A look around

## Features **The loop** - **Dual-agent architecture** — planning and review (Mentor) kept apart from execution (Executor) - **Smart coordination** — structured handoff prompts, quality gates and smart pauses keep iterations focused - **Acceptance checks** — the Mentor runs tests and lint, then returns a verdict with risk, evidence and a next step - **Plan gate and iteration cap** — optionally approve the first plan yourself, and cap iterations per pair (runs are unbounded by default) - **Stall detection** — a warning after 120 s without output, stalled after 600 s **The console** - **One session console** — task, plans, results, reviews and live turns in a single scrollable feed, with search and role filters - **Cognitive event stream** — intent chips, reasoning steps and tool-call status for every turn - **Usage tracking** — tokens per turn and per run, estimated cost, request count and last output - **Inspector** — collapsible sections for models, run state, usage, files, history and timeline - **Activity and Insights** — what needs attention across all pairs, and which model combinations have worked **Your repository** - **Git change tracking** — added, modified and deleted files against a baseline commit, with an inline diff for each - **Worktrees** — run each task in its own git worktree on a `the-pair/…` branch, then commit and push from the inspector - **Skills and mentions** — attach project skill files with `/skill` and files with `@path` - **Session recovery** — snapshots are saved as you go; Is The Pair free and open source? Yes. The Pair is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and free to download for macOS, Windows and Linux. You pay only for your own model usage — or run local models with [Ollama](https://ollama.com) for no API cost.
Is it an alternative to Cursor, GitHub Copilot or Aider? Yes, with a different approach. Those tools drive a single agent. The Pair runs two independent agents — a read-only Mentor and an Executor — that cross-check each other, so a mistake is caught by a second model instead of shipped. It is local-first, open source and model-agnostic.
Which models work? Any model reachable through an endpoint you connect — imported from another agent's configuration, added by hand, or signed in with a subscription — including GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, GLM, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax and DeepSeek, plus local models via Ollama. Mix them freely, for example Claude as Mentor and GPT as Executor.
Does it need an internet connection? The app runs locally. Only the model calls need connectivity, and with Ollama not even those.
Can I control how much the agents think? Yes. For models that offer it, set the reasoning effort for the Mentor and the Executor independently, when you create the pair or later from its settings.
Can I see what an agent is actually doing? Yes. Each turn shows a stream of cognitive events — intent chips, reasoning steps, and each tool call with its status — so you can follow the agent's logic without reading raw output.
How do I track tokens and cost? Usage is tracked per turn, with input and output broken out. Live counts appear in the console, the inspector and the exported run report.
What if an agent gets stuck in a loop? Runs are unbounded by default. If you set an iteration cap, reaching it pauses the run into **Awaiting Human Review**, where you can continue, reassign or finish. A per-turn step-cycle guard also stops runaway tool loops.
What if the app crashes or I close it mid-session? Session snapshots are saved automatically. On the next launch The Pair finds interrupted sessions and offers to restore them with their full history.
Does it update itself? Yes. The Pair checks for a new version on launch and installs it in one click.

## Design Context

### Users

Developer-professionals who want automated AI pair programming with cross-validation. They're concerned about AI hallucinations and want confidence in generated code. Context: working on serious projects, want to delegate routine coding while maintaining oversight. Job to be done: run two AI agents that check each other's work so they can focus on review rather than constant intervention.

### Brand Personality

**Precision • Thoughtfulness • Modern**

The brand evokes confidence and trust in AI-generated code. Not playful or experimental—serious tooling for serious work. Refined aesthetic with glass/metal effects signals premium, polished experience. Voice is clear, direct, technical without being cold.

### Aesthetic Direction

**Refined glassmorphism** with metal sheen accents. Subtle gradients, blur effects, grain overlay for texture. Light mode is airy with blue-purple radial accents; dark mode is sophisticated with subtle glow effects. Typography: Geist Sans (display), Geist Mono (code/data). Status colors: blue (mentoring), purple (executing), amber (paused/reviewing), green (finished/ready).

**References**: Linear, Arc browser—premium tooling aesthetic
**Anti-references**: Generic SaaS gradients, cartoonish icons, heavy shadows

### Design Principles

1. **Trust through transparency** — Show agent activity, resource usage, git changes visibly so users understand what's happening
2. **Subtle sophistication** — Glass effects and metal accents feel premium without being flashy; animations are smooth, not bouncy
3. **Information density with clarity** — Compact cards pack data but remain readable through hierarchy, truncation, and consistent spacing
4. **Status-driven visuals** — Color coding (blue/purple/amber/green) makes pair state instantly scannable
5. **Responsive refinement** — Works beautifully from single column mobile to three-column desktop; spacing scales appropriately

## [3.0.4] - 2026-11-14

### Fixed

- **Restoring or reloading a pair no longer rewinds live work.** Backend state wins over stale renderer snapshots, crash recovery keeps the selected endpoint, conversation and run position, and an unreadable snapshot is quarantined without hiding healthy pairs.
- **Failed turns recover without corrupting the conversation.** Retry and cooldown waits are cancellable, spent quotas do not throttle unrelated calls, context overflow pauses with compacted history, and tool-call history stays replayable. Backup-model usage is attributed to the endpoint that actually answered.
- **Completion requires verifiable work.** Empty diffs, missing review evidence, and checks that time out, fail to start or exit unknown can no longer pass acceptance. The Mentor must provide explicit confidence, and its parsed checklist reaches the Executor.
- **Run changes preserve workspace work and accurate diffs.** Each run keeps a fixed Git baseline, stale monitor samples cannot overwrite a new run, replacement worktrees are created before old ones are removed, and a stop timeout pauses instead of deleting the workspace. Rescue cleanup only removes branches already contained elsewhere.
- **Console controls and token usage stay consistent.** Control commands are locked per pair with state-event fallback, handoffs remain visible and bounded, token fields merge without stale values, snapshot and diff failures surface in the UI, and file diffs use the run baseline.

## [3.0.0] - 2026-11-11

Pairs talk to model endpoints directly instead of spawning agent CLIs, and a Models section is where credentials now live.

### Changed

- **Every turn is made by the app itself.** A pair connects straight to the model endpoint over HTTPS — no agent CLI is spawned, so nothing has to be installed or signed in outside the app. You pick an endpoint, a model and a reasoning effort; the pair keeps the model id and its effort, and the endpoint and credential are resolved when a turn starts.
- **A Models section in the left rail.** It lists every endpoint the app can reach with its accounts and models, and it is where you add a key, import the configuration another agent already has (kimi, pi, omp, opencode, codex, claude, gemini, killi) or sign in with a ChatGPT, Command Code, OpenCode Go or Muse Code subscription. Endpoints with no usable credential are listed too, with the state that blocks them.
- **The Executor runs its own tools.** read / grep / glob / write / edit / bash (+ todo_write) execute inside the app and are gated per role — the Mentor stays read-only.
- **The model picker is endpoint-first.** Step one is the endpoint that runs the model, step two the model, step three the reasoning effort. An endpoint you have no credential for is shown with its state instead of hidden.
- **The inspector reports usage instead of machine load.** Its usage section shows tokens per turn and per run, an estimated cost, the number of requests and the last output.

### Removed

- **Aider and Kiro support.** Neither has a channel any more; they are not part of the registry.
- **Per-agent CPU and memory monitoring.** The token and cost figures above replace it.

### Fixed

- **A Command Code or Responses endpoint could not answer at all.** The transport refused Command Code's `application/x-ndjson` replies as "not an event stream", so every turn on that gateway failed before it started; its bare-JSON-per-line stream is read now. A Codex `[model_providers.*]` entry is a Responses endpoint whichever way its `wire_api` is spelled, and Kimi's own `type = "kimi"` providers are importable instead of skipped as "account login".
- **A token that was refreshed once could never be used again.** The rotated refresh token was never written back, so the next sign-in spent the spent one and the flow gave up for good. It is persisted now, and a failed refresh keeps the client registration instead of forcing a new one.
- **An account that hit a 401 stayed expired forever.** The status was recomputed from the secret it had just been replaced with, so re-signing in never cleared it. Expiry is now honoured, pasting a key onto an OAuth account makes it ready, and a credential that flips between a live variable and a key keeps one account instead of two.
- **The Models badge was always zero until you opened Models.** The store behind it only loaded when the section mounted; it loads at startup now.
- **A model change did not reach the run in progress.** `pair_update_models` rewrote the stored id but left the resolved selection in place, so resuming kept talking to the old endpoint. The changed role's selection is dropped and resolved again.
- **A model id that a gateway lists was refused.** The vendor hint excluded any endpoint that was not named for that vendor, so an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` proxy or OpenRouter could not serve a `claude-*` id even though it listed it. An endpoint that lists the id wins now.
- **A model could not be picked on a gateway at all.** The same hint made `pair_create` roll back with "The mentor has no model selected" and re-picking never helped.
- **The reasoning effort you picked was never sent.** The pair's per-role effort was persisted and shown in the picker but never reached the request; the route default was sent instead.
- **Streaming a reply re-sent the whole pair state once per token.** A 4k-token answer serialized the full state 4,000 times over IPC. Activity and reasoning updates are paced now, and the state a turn ends with is still published.
- **A torn tool call poisoned every later turn of that run.** Arguments cut mid-stream were stored verbatim and replayed as invalid JSON, which every API rejects permanently. They are repaired before they are stored, and a failed attempt's partial output is discarded rather than counted twice.
- **A huge repetition count in a search pattern could exhaust memory.** `a{100000000}` compiled to 100M instructions (~4 GB) before any matching ran; the compiler refuses a count it cannot honour now.
- **A path that is not a regular file could hang a turn forever.** `read`/`edit` blocked on a FIFO with no timeout and no way to cancel. The file work runs off the async worker now, and writes go through a temp file so a failed write leaves the original whole.
- **The mentor's review could hang on a long reply.** Every balanced `{…}` in it was parsed; the scan is linear now and bounded.
- **The import wizard reported the wrong endpoint for a Codex gateway and dropped Kimi's own providers.** Codex has one wire protocol (Responses), so its custom gateways no longer post to `/chat/completions`; Kimi's `type = "kimi"` is Moonshot's OpenAI-compatible interface and imports with a key.
- **API keys exported in a shell profile were invisible.** A GUI launch inherits no profile, so every env-backed account read as unset and its turn failed with "not set in this shell". The login shell's whole environment is captured at startup now.
- **A key imported from another agent could panic the Models section.** Secrets were masked by byte offsets, which is not a character boundary for a non-ASCII key; and an endpoint whose URL normalises to nothing panicked inside a Tauri command.
- **The Model picker forgot the model you had just picked.** Switching endpoint and back landed on an older recent model; the recent list is live now.
- **A sign-in that failed left its state behind.** Closing the dialog and reopening it showed the stale error with the service still selected, so three of four buttons stayed disabled. The flow resets on open.
- **A base URL you typed with no scheme was accepted.** The add-provider form refuses anything without a host, and an unusable one comes back as a message instead of a panic.
- **Assigning a task could destroy the transcript.** A failed start cleared the run's messages before it knew the models resolved; both selections are resolved first now, and a pair that cannot be resumed comes back paused with the reason instead of dead.
- **Reloading the pair list mid-run rewinded a live pair.** Its turn cancelled itself and the pair hung with nothing running. A pair that is live here is never overwritten from disk.
- **Usage was counted twice for a turn.** The console hides the duplicate turn card but the inspector summed both copies; tokens, cost and request counts now match the transcript.
- **Two cognitive events in the same millisecond shared an id**, producing duplicate React keys in the timeline; ids carry a per-role sequence now.
- **A glob whose star components explode no longer hangs**, and a repetition count above what the matcher can honour is refused instead of allocating.

# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

- **Demonstrating empathy and kindness** toward other people
- **Being respectful of differing opinions**, viewpoints, and experiences
- **Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback**
- **Accepting responsibility and apologizing** to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
- **Focusing on what is best** not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

- **The use of sexualized language or imagery**, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
- **Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments**, and personal or political attacks
- **Public or private harassment**
- **Publishing others' private information**, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
- **Other conduct** which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at:

- **GitHub**: [timwuhaotian](https://github.com/timwuhaotian)
- **Email**: [Create an issue for contact](https://github.com/timwuhaotian/the-pair/issues/new)

All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, during this period is allowed. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage], version 2.1, available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html][v2.1].

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by [Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][Mozilla CoC].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq][FAQ]. Translations are available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations][translations].

# The Pair

> The Pair is a free, open-source AI pair programming desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It runs two AI coding agents on one task: a read-only Mentor that plans and reviews, and an Executor that writes code, runs commands, and verifies the result.

The main value is cross-validated AI code review. Instead of asking one model to write and self-review, The Pair separates planning, implementation, and review so another agent can catch hallucinations, missing tests, unsafe edits, or incomplete work before changes reach the codebase.

Since version 3.0 the app talks to model endpoints directly over HTTPS and runs the agents' tools itself. No agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, opencode or any other) has to be installed.

## Key Facts

- Two agents collaborate in one local desktop app.
- The Mentor is read-only and reviews the Executor's work.
- The Executor writes code and runs verification commands, scoped to the pair's workspace.
- Mentor and Executor can be different models, each with its own reasoning effort — for example Claude as Mentor and GPT as Executor.
- Runs continue until the mentor signals completion or a human stops them; an optional per-pair iteration cap pauses for human review when reached.
- Activity tracking warns after 120 seconds without agent output and marks the agent stalled after 600 seconds.
- Sessions can recover after app restart with conversation history and turn state.
- Each task can run in its own git worktree, and changed files are tracked against a baseline commit with inline diffs.
- Token usage, estimated cost and request counts are tracked per turn and per run.
- Credentials stay in the app's own local store; there is no account system, relay server or telemetry.
- The interface is available in English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

## Common Questions

- Is The Pair free? Yes. It is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to download.
- Does it need Claude Code, Codex or another CLI installed? No. It needs one model endpoint with a credential.
- Which models work? Any model behind an endpoint you connect, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, GLM, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax and DeepSeek, plus local models via Ollama.
- Does it work offline? The app runs locally; only model calls need a network, and with Ollama not even those.
- How is it different from Cursor, GitHub Copilot or Aider? Those drive a single agent that reviews its own output. The Pair gives review to a second, read-only agent.

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

A Tauri 2 desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) whose UI is a React web view. The design language is the app's own, not native platform chrome. Minimum window width is 1200px (`src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`).

## Users

Developers who already work with AI coding tools and models, and who may already have endpoints configured inside another agent's install. The primary scene is **watching and steering live**: The Pair sits open beside the editor, the developer reads the Mentor and Executor as they work, and steps in by stopping a turn, sending feedback, approving or sending back a plan, or reassigning models.

Hand-off-and-return ("grab a coffee") is a supported secondary workflow and part of the marketing story, but design decisions favor the live-steering scene first.

## Product Purpose

Run two AI coding agents against one task so they cross-check each other: a read-only **Mentor** plans and reviews, and an **Executor** writes code and runs commands. One model writing and judging its own work misses its own mistakes; an independent reviewer catches them before they reach the codebase. Success means the developer gets reviewed, validated changes with less babysitting and keeps control at every decision point.

## Positioning

- Two independent agents with separated roles (read-only reviewer plus writer), not one assistant reviewing itself.
- Model-agnostic and local: it connects straight to model endpoints over HTTPS — importing endpoints and credentials from other agents' configs or adding them by hand — and any model can fill either role (for example Claude as Mentor and GPT as Executor).
- Open source (Apache 2.0) and free. A terminal companion, Pair Code (`pair-code` on npm), covers terminal, script, and SSH workflows.

## Operating Context

- Lives next to the code editor during a working session, often for long-running pairs.
- Works in a local git repository: tracks modified files against a baseline commit, shows inline diffs, commits and pushes, and can run each task in a fresh worktree on an auto-named branch.
- Turn loop: Idle → Mentoring → Executing → Reviewing → (loop | Finished | Paused | Awaiting Human Review | Error). An optional plan gate pauses after the Mentor's first plan for human approval. An optional per-pair iteration cap pauses for human review when reached; runs are unbounded by default.
- Tracks per-role token usage, estimated cost and request counts, detects stalled turns, and restores full session state after a restart or crash.

## Capabilities and Constraints

- A model registry of endpoints, each with a protocol (OpenAI Chat, Anthropic Messages, Responses, Gemini-compatible, Command Code), accounts and model routes. Endpoints are discovered by importing other agents' configs or added by hand; users pick an endpoint, then a model and a reasoning effort for each role.
- Pair console: one transcript of task, plans, results, acceptance checks, human feedback, and live turn cards with tool-call and reasoning steps. Includes search, role filters, task history, and archived runs.
- Acceptance: the Mentor runs checks (tests, lint, and so on) and returns a structured verdict (pass/fail, risk, evidence, next step).
- Presets, skills (`/skill`), and file mentions (`@path`) attach context to tasks.
- Fixed terminology, never renamed or paraphrased in any locale: **Pair**, **Mentor**, **Executor**. A "task" is what the user gives a pair; "acceptance" is the Mentor's check of the Executor's work; "plan review" is the human approval gate.
- Mock mode (`THE_PAIR_E2E_MOCK=true`) runs the UI without live model calls.

## Brand Commitments

- **Terminal/TTY voice:** mono, terse, ASCII rules (`── checks ──`), glyph markers, compact uppercase tags. This is the product's identity, not decoration to remove.
- **Light humor stays:** lines such as "Mentor plans. Executor ships." and "grab a coffee" belong to the voice. Humor never appears in errors, destructive confirmations, or blocked work.
- **Four equal locales:** English, 简体中文, 日本語, and 한국어 are all first-class. Every new user-facing string ships in all four.
- Name "The Pair", the app icon (`docs/assets/app-icon.svg`), and the logo (`resources/logo-the-pair.png`).

## Product Principles

1. **The human steers.** Every automated step leaves a clear point to pause, stop, approve, or redirect, and the current state is always legible at a glance.
2. **Show the work.** Agent reasoning, tool calls, checks, and verdicts are surfaced plainly so the developer can trust or challenge them.
3. **Roles stay distinct.** Mentor and Executor are always visually and verbally distinguishable; the separation is the product.
4. **Bring your own models.** No endpoint is privileged; any model you connect can fill either role.
5. **Local and recoverable.** Work stays on the user's machine and in their git history, and sessions survive interruption.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

WCAG 2.2 AA is the floor for every surface: text contrast, full keyboard operation, visible focus, and screen-reader names that match visible labels. Role and state are never conveyed by color alone. All four locales must survive text expansion at the minimum window width.

# Code Signing & Notarization

This document provides detailed instructions for code signing and notarizing The Pair for macOS distribution.

## Release Flow Overview

The repository uses a GitHub Actions release pipeline:

```
push to main
  → detect package.json version bump
  → run lint, typecheck, and tests
  → build macOS/Windows/Linux release artifacts
  → codesign and notarize the macOS bundle
  → package ZIP on macOS plus Windows/Linux installers
  → create/update GitHub Release with all platform assets
```

The workflow file is: [build-signed-mac.yml](../.github/workflows/build-signed-mac.yml)

## What You Need from Apple

### 1. Apple Developer Program Membership

Apple's Developer ID docs state that software distributed outside the Mac App Store uses a Developer ID certificate plus notarization.

### 2. Developer ID Application Certificate

1. Sign in to `developer.apple.com`
2. Open `Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles`
3. Create a `Developer ID Application` certificate
4. Download the `.cer`
5. Double-click it to install it into Keychain Access

### 3. Export the Certificate as `.p12`

In Keychain Access:

1. Find `Developer ID Application: ...`
2. Export it as `.p12`
3. Set an export password

### 4. Apple ID App-Specific Password

Needed because the workflow uses `xcrun notarytool --apple-id --password --team-id`.

1. Go to `account.apple.com` → `Sign-In and Security` → `App-Specific Passwords`
2. Create a new app-specific password

### 5. Apple Team ID

Found under `Membership details` in your developer account.

## GitHub Actions Secrets

Configure these in `Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions`:

| Secret                               | What it is                                                              | How to get it                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `MACOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY`             | Exact signing identity string used by Tauri as `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | Run `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` after installing the certificate, then copy the `Developer ID Application: ...` line |
| `MACOS_CERTIFICATE_P12_BASE64`       | Base64-encoded `.p12` export of your Developer ID Application cert      | `base64 -i /path/to/developer-id.p12 \| pbcopy` on macOS                                                                            |
| `MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`         | Password you chose when exporting the `.p12`                            | You set this during export                                                                                                          |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`          | Tauri updater signing private key, stored as file contents or a path    | Generate it with `npm run tauri signer generate -- -w ~/.tauri/the-pair.key` and copy the private key into the secret               |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the updater private key, if you generated one              | Use the same password you passed to `tauri signer generate`                                                                         |
| `APPLE_ID`                           | Apple Account email used for notarization                               | Your Apple Developer account email                                                                                                  |
| `APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD`        | App-specific password for notarization                                  | Go to `account.apple.com` → `Sign-In and Security` → `App-Specific Passwords`                                                       |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID`                      | 10-character Apple team identifier                                      | `developer.apple.com` → `Membership details`                                                                                        |

**Notes:**

- GitHub's built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` is already used for creating/updating releases in the main repo. You do **not** need to add that one manually.
- The updater private key is the gatekeeper for shipping new versions to existing users. If you lose it, you can still ship a new app binary, but you must rotate the updater key pair and update `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` with the new public key before the release can go out.

## Local Signed Build

For local release builds, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in:

```bash
export CSC_NAME="Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
export CSC_KEY_PASSWORD="your-p12-password"
export CSC_LINK="/absolute/path/to/developer-id.p12"
export APPLE_ID="your-apple-id@example.com"

The local macOS build flow keeps the DMG-style installer you prefer. If you want to locally reproduce the ZIP-style release asset, run `npm run build:mac:release`. The release workflow still publishes ZIP assets to GitHub Releases for stability. The build flow will install the required Rust targets automatically when `rustup` is available. If you need to do it yourself, run:

```bash
rustup target add aarch64-apple-darwin x86_64-apple-darwin
```

- macOS: `the-pair-{version}.zip`
- Windows: `the-pair-{version}-setup.exe`
- Linux: `the-pair-{version}.AppImage.tar.gz` (extract, then run the AppImage)

## Manual Notarization Check

If you want to verify notarization manually:

```bash
APP_PATH=$(find dist -maxdepth 3 -name "*.app" | head -n 1)
ZIP_PATH="dist/the-pair-{version}.zip"

ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc --keepParent "$APP_PATH" "$ZIP_PATH"

xcrun notarytool submit "$ZIP_PATH" \
  --apple-id "$APPLE_ID" \
  --password "$APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD" \
  --team-id "$TEAM_ID" \
  --wait

xcrun stapler staple "$APP_PATH"
xcrun stapler validate "$APP_PATH"
```

## Verify Signature

```bash
APP_PATH=$(find dist -maxdepth 3 -name "*.app" | head -n 1)
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 "$APP_PATH"
```

- A `Developer ID Application` certificate
- Notarization credentials (`APPLE_ID`, app-specific password, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`)

### What You **Do Not** Need

- App Store app record
- TestFlight setup
- Provisioning profile for App Store distribution

The only App Store Connect-related case you may care about is team management. Apple notes that, for Apple Developer Program organizations, team member access is managed in App Store Connect. If you are a solo developer, you can ignore that.

# Harness Migration Plan（CLI 派生 → 直连模型）

The Pair 从「spawn 各 agent 的 CLI」改造为「自建 harness，按 model-to-model 直连模型供应商」。
参照实现：`../killi`（同作者的 Rust CLI harness，含 LLM 传输层、配置导入、OAuth 登录、工具循环）。

## 0. 目标与非目标

### 目标（可验证的验收）

1. 不 spawn 任何 agent CLI；每个 turn 由 the-pair 自己的 HTTP 客户端直连模型供应商。
2. 供应商发现覆盖：kimi / pi / omp / opencode / codex / claude / gemini 的配置文件 + the-pair 现有 agent 配置 + `~/.killi/config.toml` + `~/.killi/chatgpt.json` + 环境变量；按 (协议, base_url) 去重。
3. OAuth 全部可在 app 内完成：ChatGPT（PKCE）、CommandCode（反向代理回传）、opencode-go（自定义 header）、muse code（key + 工具名映射）。
4. executor 自带工具循环（read / grep / glob / write / edit / bash + todo_write），mentor 只读。
5. pair 编排层语义不变：acceptance、quality_gate、context_bridge、smart_pause、session_snapshot/recovery、intelligence_store、iteration cap、stall 检测。
6. 旧 pair 快照尽力自动迁移；无法映射的标「需配置」并暂停等人类。

### 非目标

- 不保留 CLI 兜底轨道，不做 hybrid 模式。
- 不做工具调用人工审批（全自动执行）。
- 不做 web 工具、subagent / swarm、MCP。
- 不做 aider、kiro（v1 从供应商清单删除）。
- 不移植 Claude Code / Antigravity 的订阅登录态。
- 不做跨 app 的 OAuth 刷新协调（接受与 killi 的竞争）。

### 2.5 移植硬风险（动手前必须解决）

1. **killi 是 bin crate，无 `lib.rs`**：搬模块时要重建模块树，`crate::` 路径全部重写。
2. **`Agent` 用 `Rc`/`RefCell`（`!Send`）**：Tauri async command 与 `tokio::spawn` 要求 `Send`。要么把 `Agent` 钉在单个 long-running task 内通过 channel 通信，要么把 `Rc` 换成 `Arc`/`Mutex`。建议前者（改动面小）。

4. **killi 无 CancellationToken**，靠进程信号取消；Tauri 侧需要显式取消通道（kill/pause 命令）。

**资源与 DoS**

- `tools/search.rs` 的重复计数只受 `usize` 限制：`a{100000000}` 编译出 1 亿条指令（实测 ~4 GB / 253 ms），`a{4294967295}` 直接 abort 整个 app。编译期拒绝超过 1000 的计数。
- `match_parts` 递归没有自己的预算，`**/`×N 的 glob 在深树上不可恢复地挂死。
- `acceptance.rs` 的 verdict 扫描是 O(n²) 且对每个平衡 `{…}` 都 `from_str`，长回复会卡住 review turn。
- `driver.rs` 每收到一个 delta 就 `notify_state_update` 一次全量 `PairState`：4k token 的回复 = 4000 次全状态 IPC 序列化。activity / reasoning 现在按 ~1s 合流，turn 结束时补一次终态。

# Release Checklist

Use this checklist before cutting a public release of The Pair.

**⚠️ CRITICAL: The release workflow is fully automated. Never manually create or push tags.**

The GitHub Actions workflow (`build-signed-mac.yml`) automatically:

- Detects version bumps in package.json
- Creates tags
- Builds all platform binaries
- Publishes GitHub releases
- Uploads signed artifacts

## 1. Repo Hygiene

- [ ] Working tree is clean except for the intended release commit
- [ ] Version bumped with `npm run bump <version>` (updates `package.json`, the root entries of `package-lock.json`, the `[package]` version in `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and the app entry in `src-tauri/Cargo.lock`; `tauri.conf.json` reads `package.json`)
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` has a non-empty `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` section, heading at the start of a line (`npm run validate:changelog` passes)
- [ ] `README.md` still matches the current install and test flow
- [ ] `LICENSE`, `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and `SECURITY.md` are present

## 2. Quality Gates

Run these commands locally before pushing the release commit:

```bash
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm run build
```

- [ ] `npm test` passes
- [ ] `npm run typecheck` passes
- [ ] `npm run lint` passes
- [ ] `npm run build` passes

## 3. Release Metadata

- [ ] `package.json` still points to the correct repository and bugs URLs
- [ ] `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` has the correct package metadata
- [ ] `docs/RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` was reviewed for any stale release process notes
- [ ] Release notes mention any breaking changes or migration steps
- [ ] `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` and optional password secrets are configured in GitHub Actions
- [ ] The updater signing key validates in CI before the build stage
- [ ] The collected updater packages pass signature verification against `plugins.updater.pubkey` in `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`

## 4. Binary Checks

- [ ] App launches locally after the build
- [ ] Icons render correctly on macOS, Windows, and Linux bundles
- [ ] Release artifacts are generated for macOS, Windows, and Linux
- [ ] `npm run preflight`, `npm run build:mac`, `npm run build:win`, or `npm run build:linux` work for the target platform

## 5. GitHub Release (Automated)

**⚠️ IMPORTANT: Do NOT create or push tags manually!**

The release workflow is fully automated:

- [ ] Push the version bump commit to main branch (`git push`)
- [ ] Wait for GitHub Actions workflow to detect version bump
- [ ] Workflow auto-creates tag and publishes release with all artifacts
- [ ] Monitor workflow at: https://github.com/timwuhaotian/the-pair/actions
- [ ] Verify the release page downloads without authentication
- [ ] Verify the release notes are readable and complete

**Workflow flow:**

1. `detect-version-bump` checks the version's tag, release and assets. It skips only a complete public release; a draft, orphan tag or incomplete release fails for manual inspection.
2. For a new version, the workflow validates the changelog, runs frontend checks and Rust tests in parallel, then builds all platforms.
3. `publish-release` verifies all three updater signatures against the app's configured public key, then rechecks the state and creates the tag and draft. It compares the uploaded assets' GitHub SHA-256 digests with the local files before publishing. Existing releases and assets are never overwritten.
4. Release runs share a concurrency group and are not cancelled mid-run. GitHub may replace an already pending run with a newer one; intermediate versions are not guaranteed to publish.

`detect-version-bump` and `publish-release` have `contents: write` (the former needs draft visibility); other jobs are read-only, and checkouts don't persist the token. The updater key and macOS certificate are removed from `$RUNNER_TEMP` by a cleanup step even on failure, although abrupt runner termination can prevent cleanup. Third-party actions (`dtolnay/rust-toolchain`, `Swatinem/rust-cache`) are pinned to commit SHAs — update the SHA and its `# version` comment together when upgrading.

If a release fails after tag creation, inspect the tag commit, draft, run artifacts and signatures. For a draft, upload only verified missing assets and publish only after checking the complete set. For an orphan tag, inspect it and choose a new version or resolve it manually. Never overwrite a public release's assets; publish fixes under a new version. The workflow does not delete tags or releases automatically.

**Manual trigger (fallback):** The selected commit must be reachable from `main`.

```bash
gh workflow run build-signed-mac.yml
```

## 6. Post-Release Verification

- [ ] Download the published artifact from GitHub Releases
- [ ] Install and launch the app from the packaged artifact
- [ ] Confirm `npm test` still passes on the release commit
- [ ] Confirm the new version is visible in the app and release page

# App icon

Source of truth (edit this, not the PNGs):

- `app-icon.svg` — the shipped app icon: navy field `#1E3049`, two tiles with a check each, coral stick, gold spark

The icon belongs to the family killi, kil and kiled share. It is killi's icon (`../killi/docs/icon.svg`) with the same field, stick, spark and colors, and two tiles where killi has one. The tiles are the brand mark's (`src/renderer/src/components/BrandMark.tsx`), which is also what the boot splash animates, so the icon in the Dock and the first thing the window shows are the same drawing.

The glyph is still the double-check (✓✓), now one check per tile: two agents each check the work once — Mentor plans/reviews, Executor writes/reviews back — which is the product promise ("reviewed, validated work").

One icon serves light and dark: the navy field reads on both, as killi's does.

`app-icon-preview.png` shows it at 256/128/64/32/16 on light and dark.

## Regenerating

magick /tmp/app-icon-956.png -background none -gravity center -extent 1024x1024 /tmp/app-icon-master.png
npx tauri icon /tmp/app-icon-master.png   # rebuilds src-tauri/icons/* (icns/ico/png/android/ios)
cp /tmp/app-icon-master.png resources/logo-the-pair.png

```
